docs.text: AgentIR 1.3.0 · Python · vLLM

docs.title: AgentIR documentation
docs.text:
Write an agent's decisions in Python. Let the runtime begin useful work before those decisions finish.

AgentIR is an intermediate representation and runtime for agent programs that generate candidates, evaluate them, and continue from a selection. It makes the difference between needing a result to build a request and needing a decision to keep that request explicit. That distinction creates opportunities to overlap work.

For example, while a judge compares three answers, AgentIR can start a continuation for each answer. Once the judge selects one, its continuation survives and the others are cancelled. The program still publishes only the selected result.

docs.title: Where AgentIR helps
docs.text:
Speculation is most useful when the program exposes a continuation before the decision selecting it finishes, and the engine has capacity to run it. Candidate search, judge-and-refine pipelines, and predictable tool observations can provide that structure. Speedup depends on decision latency, surviving work, cache reuse, and contention; it is a measurement, not a runtime guarantee.

AgentIR's branch speculation and vLLM's draft-token decoding operate at different levels. Either can be enabled independently. See the four optimization mechanisms before interpreting an experiment.

Need a specific name or default? Open the Python API, runtime configuration, CLI, or glossary.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
AgentIR turns a Python agent program into a graph of model requests, Python operations, tool executions, and decisions. The tracer constructs that graph while the runtime executes its ready parts. A request may start before its keep-or-cancel decision is known, but only after its input data exists.

This page follows one invocation through the system. You do not need the internal types to use the first program.

The solid arrows carry requests or data. The dashed return path resolves decisions and dependencies. Static shape compilation is optional. Open the full diagram.

docs.title: 1. A program describes possible work
docs.text:
A typical program has four operations:

  1. Generate candidate answers with expand.
  2. Evaluate them with a Python op or another model request.
  3. Rank candidate indices with choose.
  4. Continue from the chosen handle with infer.

The program manipulates handles, not generated strings. A handle preserves how its prompt was built, which requests it depends on, and which decisions must eventually select it. This gives the runtime enough information to schedule safely.

docs.title: 2. The tracer builds a guarded graph
docs.text:
The tracer lowers model calls into engine nodes, tools into tool nodes, and selections into decisions. Python operations produce asynchronous values on the control plane. A guard describes the decisions under which a node survives.

Consider a judge choosing between answers A and B. The continuation of A needs A's text. It does not need the judge's text to construct its prompt. Its connection to the judge is a keep-or-cancel condition.

When infer receives an unresolved choice, the tracer creates a continuation for every possible selected member, each with its own guard. This transformation is called hoisting. It is the central source of branch speculation.

Connection Example What execution waits for Data dependency A continuation includes answer A A's output must exist Control dependency Keep A's continuation only if the judge chooses A The decision must resolve before commitment; execution may begin earlier Effect ordering Run a tool after another operation settles The predecessor must settle; the tool's own effect contract still applies

docs.title: 3. The scheduler chooses ready work
docs.text:
The scheduler runs on a dedicated event-loop thread. It gives committed requests priority, then funds eligible speculative requests within a guard-depth window and a concurrency budget.

Engine adapters own model execution and cancellation. The in-process adapter uses vLLM's request API and automatic prefix caching. A separate tool scheduler and worker pool execute Python tools. The runtime also owns tracer and control-plane worker pools, so waiting for a tool does not occupy an engine request slot.

The scheduler never obtains missing input bytes by guessing across a data dependency. Tool observation prediction works by explicitly constructing candidate observations, then guarding their continuations with a later verification decision.

docs.title: 4. Results resolve decisions
docs.text:
An engine request can finish while its guard is still unresolved. Its output is available to eligible speculative descendants, but the request is not yet committed.

When a decision resolves, surviving work can commit. Losing work is squashed, and running engine requests are cancelled. A public force(...) waits for both the relevant data and its publication conditions. Unknown-effect Python operations and tools wait for commitment before running their bodies.

An illustrative schedule, not a benchmark. The overlap is useful only if the surviving continuation gains more time than speculation costs in contention. Open the full diagram.

docs.title: 5. Diagnostics explain the outcome
docs.text:
The ledger records when each node registered, became ready, issued, finished, and resolved its guard. It distinguishes committed, wasted, and failed work. Timelines visualize these events; differential checks compare the selected computation with an independent serial execution.

A completed request, a committed request, and a faster invocation are three different observations. The verification section explains how to establish each.

docs.title: Models and vLLM
docs.text: AgentIR's local engine adapter targets vLLM 0.24.0. It submits independent generation requests with stable seeds and priorities, and uses vLLM's automatic prefix caching to reuse prompt work. There is no separate copy-on-write engine-fork primitive in this adapter.

docs.title: Create a runtime
docs.text:
from agentir import SpecConfig, make_runtime

runtime = make_runtime(
    model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
    max_inflight=32,
    engine_args={"max_model_len": 2048, "gpu_memory_utilization": 0.5},
    spec=SpecConfig(window=2, max_spec_inflight=8),
)

Weights load lazily on first use or explicit warmup. Call runtime.close() when finished, or use with make_runtime(...) as runtime:. Keep runtime creation behind a Python main guard when using subprocess engines.

max_inflight limits AgentIR requests on a physical engine. The effective capacity also respects an explicitly supplied vLLM max_num_seqs. The adapter requires priority scheduling; committed work must be able to outrank speculation.

docs.title: Choose a wire
Give models explicit roles
docs.text:
make_runtime creates a main role and, by default, aliases judge to it. Supply judge_model for a separate judge engine. devices and judge_devices select the GPU visibility of the respective engines.

For more roles, construct Runtime from ModelSpec and EngineSpec configurations. Unknown role names raise an error. Physical engines are deduplicated by their resolved configuration, including model, device placement, parser settings, and token drafter configuration.

Multiple engines can share a token-wire runtime. Their token spaces must be compatible: identical model identity is a fast path; otherwise the runtime compares tokenizer fingerprints, including backend configuration and special-token IDs. Matching vocabulary size alone is insufficient.

judge_process=True runs the judge behind a managed server process; judge_server_attach connects to an existing one. These judge-server modes require the text wire and serve the scoring workflow. They are distinct from the certified remote runtime.

docs.title: Freeze generation and template settings
docs.text:
Sampling parameters are validated and frozen before node identity is constructed. Use max_tokens, temperature, top_p, and the other supported parameters. The DSL derives the sampling seed from identity; it does not accept an arbitrary per-call seed.

Chat template options are also captured as canonical configuration. Supply chat_template_kwargs for the main model and judge_chat_template_kwargs for the judge. Omitted judge options inherit the main options; an explicit {} resets them.

For constrained generation, structured accepts exactly one supported constraint kind. Capabilities are checked before a request can rely on them. A parser or template incompatibility should surface as an error, not a silently altered prompt.

docs.title: Understand event granularity
docs.text:
With event_granularity="auto", ordinary committed generations can use terminal-only events. Requests watched by streamed projections, prefix prefetch, or bound policies need intermediate updates. Event granularity changes observation cost, not the semantic output contract.

The adapter preserves engine-provided text sidecars where needed; decoding the same token tuple in a different context can change visible formatting. Token and text checks therefore serve different purposes.

docs.title: Distinguish two forms of speculation
docs.text:
AgentIR speculates over agent branches. vLLM token drafting speculates over tokens inside one request. Configure drafting through the engine configuration independently of SpecConfig.enabled.

The adapter normalizes drafter configuration into engine identity and rejects incompatible sampling options. In particular, draft-enabled requests cannot include min_p or logit_bias, even when their supplied values appear neutral. See optimization mechanisms.

Source: engine.py, runtime.py, and chat_template.py.

docs.title: Work on the documentation
docs.text: The manual is an English MkDocs site using Material for navigation, search, syntax highlighting, and responsive layout. Content lives in docs/; the build does not import vLLM or require a GPU.

docs.title: Preview locally
docs.text:
From the repository root:

python3 -m venv .venv-docs
source .venv-docs/bin/activate
python -m pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
python -m mkdocs serve

Open the address printed by MkDocs, normally http://127.0.0.1:8000/AgentIR/. The /AgentIR/ prefix mirrors the configured project-site URL. Editing a page rebuilds the preview.

docs.title: Build and check
docs.text:
python -m mkdocs build --strict
python scripts/check_docs.py

The build writes the static website to site/. Strict mode checks navigation and Markdown links. The additional checker validates generated local links and fragments, repository source links, English article content, Python snippet syntax, public API coverage, and the engine-free compilation tutorial. It does not run GPU examples or fetch datasets.

The documentation workflow runs these commands and uploads the site as a build artifact. It does not publish automatically.

docs.title: Publish the website
docs.text:
The live manual is hosted at hemlix.me/AgentIR/. Its static output is published in the AgentIR/ directory of the sunyxedu.github.io repository, whose existing GitHub Pages configuration serves hemlix.me.

After a successful strict build and documentation check, replace that directory with the contents of site/, review the generated-file diff, and commit and push it to the website repository's master branch. Keep the site's root homepage, résumé, and CNAME intact. Wait for the Pages deployment to succeed and check the live overview, a nested page, and search assets before announcing publication.

The AgentIR repository keeps the editable documentation source; the website repository keeps the published build. Both commits should identify the same documentation release. To host elsewhere, update site_url before building so canonical URLs and sitemaps use the actual origin.

docs.title: Put information where readers expect it
docs.text:
Section Reader's question Writing approach Start here What is this system, and how do I run one program? Introduce architecture, then one complete example Build programs How do I accomplish a task? State prerequisites, show code, explain its result Understand the design Why does this behavior hold? Explain invariants and the implementation choices enforcing them Verify and measure How do I know it is correct or useful? Separate evidence, interpretation, and limits Reference What is the exact contract or default? Group related names; make constraints easy to scan Contribute Where is the code, and how do I change it? Map behaviors to source and focused tests

The organization borrows the staged, diagram-led navigation of AFL++, the compact concept–example–topic progression of tradingflow, and the separation of learning, reference, and deeper topics in Rust's documentation index. The diagrams and AgentIR explanations are original to this manual.

docs.title: Keep the presentation quiet
docs.text:
Use one purpose per page, short introductory paragraphs, descriptive headings, and tables only for genuine comparisons or mappings. Explain a term before relying on it. Keep configuration inventories in reference pages and place important caveats beside the feature they qualify.

The stylesheet uses local system fonts and a restrained light palette. Diagrams are versioned SVG with accessible titles, descriptions, and Markdown alternatives. The overview's stage links work with normal browser navigation and keyboard focus. A small overrides/partials/source.html template keeps the repository link static, without fetching GitHub statistics. Avoid external diagram renderers or fonts that make reading depend on another service.

docs.title: Keep examples and contracts current
docs.text:
Check the implementation and relevant tests before editing a behavior claim. Prefer the supported root exports; use canonical modules for advanced APIs. Label partial snippets and illustrative schedules. Never present an unexecuted GPU example as a measured result.

requirements-docs.in declares direct build dependencies; requirements-docs.txt pins their resolved dependency set. To refresh it with uv:

uv pip compile requirements-docs.in -o requirements-docs.txt

Rebuild strictly and repeat the browser checks after changing theme dependencies, layout, diagrams, or navigation. Check desktop and narrow mobile screens, search, sidebar navigation, keyboard focus, code copying, and the deployed subpath.

docs.title: Preserve research records
docs.text:
Frozen preregistrations stay in the repository. They are excluded from the public site's page and search indexes through exclude_docs; the experiment archive supplies English context and links to the relevant records.

Do not rewrite a preregistration to match a new experiment. Create a new versioned protocol, and update the archive map. Current backend guides should describe current code rather than inheriting older protocol assumptions.

docs.title: Compilation and algorithms
docs.text:
compile/tracer.py runs symbolic shape tracing. symbols.py defines symbolic values and graph breaks; fold.py identifies repeated regions; graph.py builds and serializes cyclic node shells and scheduling plans. test_compile_shape and test_compile_plan check structure, folding, identity parity, and funding behavior.

The eight files in algos implement self-consistency, best-of-N, beam search, SAL beam, reflexion, MCTS, heavy, and cascade. common.py provides prompts, parsers, normalization, and ranking. test_algo_traces, test_common, test_beam_judge_scorer, and test_fasttts_parts cover these layers. Read the algorithm guide before treating their graphs as interchangeable.

docs.text:

Corresponding suites include test_reference, test_scheduler_differential, test_slow_tool_audit, and test_viz.

In bench, tasks.py loads datasets, runner.py manages benchmark arms and records, stats.py provides paired statistics, and prm.py builds reward-model scoring requests. gpu_telemetry.py and vllm_metrics_telemetry.py collect resource samples; terminal_drafter_evidence.py validates shared evidence contracts.

docs.title: Integrations, examples, and experiment scripts
docs.text:
integrations/harbor/protocol.py defines the runner/environment boundary, agent.py implements Harbor's adapter and ATIF persistence, and runner.py builds and caches the actual AgentIR runtime and shell tool. The three test_harbor_* suites cover the boundary, adapter, and runner.

examples/quickstart.py is the small complete program. examples/subagent_as_tool.py covers nested invocations, leaf tools, and predicted summaries.

The larger scripts directory groups experimental drivers, analyzers, frozen locks, model probes, Slurm launchers, and cluster wrappers. Use the experiment archive to choose a family. The test_ordinary_*, test_terminal_*, test_analyze_*, and test_bench_tools_* suites validate their manifests, analysis eligibility, and orchestration boundaries.

docs.title: Make a change at the right layer
docs.text:
If a prompt identity changes, start with core identity and serial parity tests. If ordering changes, inspect both the engine and tool scheduler and effect-drain behavior. If a parser changes, check streamed prefixes, terminal agreement, retries, and the certificate contract. If an analysis changes, preserve its declared unit of comparison and validate raw-artifact provenance.

Run the focused tests for the changed boundary before a real-engine experiment. Update the corresponding explanation and reference entry when a public contract changes.

docs.title: Static shape compilation
docs.text:
shape_trace executes a program over symbolic values to discover its structure without loading a model or running Python op bodies. It produces a cyclic, parametric graph that can explain the program and optionally guide speculative funding.

It is a supported module in this checkout: agentir.compile. There is no agentir compile CLI subcommand.

docs.title: Compile a small program
docs.text:
This example runs with only the base AgentIR installation:

from agentir import cat, choose, collect, expand, force, infer, lit, op, out_text
from agentir.compile import shape_trace


def rank_by_length(answers):
    return sorted(range(len(answers)), key=lambda i: len(answers[i]))


def program(question):
    candidates = expand(lit(question), 3, max_tokens=64)
    answers = collect([out_text(candidate) for candidate in candidates])
    ranking = op(rank_by_length, answers, pure=True)
    best = choose(candidates, by=ranking, k=1)[0]
    final = infer(cat(best, lit("\nSummarize:")), max_tokens=32)
    return force(out_text(final))


graph = shape_trace(program, "Explain prefix caching.")
print(graph.summary())
with open("program-shape.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as output:
    output.write(graph.to_json())

The result describes generation shells, a ranking operation, a selection, and guarded continuations. No answer was generated, and rank_by_length was not evaluated on model outputs.

docs.title: Read the graph
docs.text:
Graph element Meaning Node shell The static part of an engine request, operation, decision, or bounded tool slot cat_data edge Prompt-spine data flows from one shell to another transform_data edge A Python operation transforms data between shells control edge A selection determines which continuation survives Loop body and back-edge Repeated structure with carried state and a trip count or bound Guard information Selection size, retained ranks, and possible continuations

The graph stores what is known before dynamic values exist. Tool-slot names and arguments, and chat-rendered tool turns, may still need runtime binding. An identity note marks cases without a fully precomputed identity prefix.

Use StaticGraph.from_json(graph.to_json()) to restore the serialized graph. Static graphs describe possible structure; runtime ledgers describe actual executions.

docs.title: Loops are represented as loops
docs.text:
The compiler recognizes repeated isomorphic blocks and folds them into a body with back-edges. It accounts for loop-carried dependencies and identity occurrence strides. A repeated candidate map should not accidentally become a temporal loop.

The explicit loop primitive can expose its body once with a bounded trip annotation. The compiler does not need to expand every possible runtime iteration into separate nodes.

docs.title: Produce an optional scheduling plan
docs.text:
from agentir import SpecConfig

spec = SpecConfig(static_plan=graph.plan())

Pass this spec to a runtime that executes the same program shape and configuration. The plan matches decision sites and provides per-decision speculation-depth and sibling-exclusivity budgets.

This is a funding plan: it does not alter guard truth, node identity, committed work, or the program's return value. A plan is also not a prediction of how long an engine request will take.

docs.title: Recognize graph breaks
docs.text:
The compiler raises GraphBreak with a source location when Python tries to inspect a symbolic value through unsupported truth conversion, length, iteration, or string materialization. It does not silently switch to a different compilation strategy.

Live chat-template rendering, dynamic Python control flow, and currently unmodeled operations such as expect or classify can also prevent shape compilation. A runtime-valid program is not necessarily statically traceable. Materialization in SAL-style search is one example of a meaningful boundary.

Keep supported computation in DSL operations if the shape is useful to compile. Otherwise run the program normally without a static plan; dynamic tracing remains the execution path.

Source: tracer.py, graph.py, fold.py, and shape tests.

docs.title: Identity and the IR
docs.text: Speculative execution changes when work runs and which attempts are cancelled. It must not silently give a surviving logical request a different prompt, sampling draw, or observation contract. AgentIR makes these properties part of the request's identity.

docs.title: A prompt is a symbolic spine
docs.text:
A Seq carries an immutable spine made of three kinds of segment:

Segment Meaning Available before the producer finishes? Lit(atoms) Literal text or token IDs Yes Out(engine_node) The generated output of an engine node Its identity is available; its output may not be Obs(tool_node, projection_id) A named projected observation of a tool Its identity is available; its image may not be

Adjacent literal segments are merged and empty literals removed. This canonical form prevents irrelevant construction differences from creating different prompt identities.

An Out segment identifies the producer symbolically. Hashing a continuation therefore does not require waiting for its producer's output bytes. At execution, that output is still a real data dependency: the prompt cannot be sent until its required atoms exist.

docs.title: Separate logical requests from physical attempts
docs.text:
An engine node's content address combines its canonical spine, model role, frozen generation parameters, sampling draw, and observation mode. Log-probability collection and tool-stream projections affect the observation contract and therefore matter to identity.

The sampling draw contains a lexical call site and scoped occurrence, plus a lane for parallel expansion. The tracer reserves it before checking branch viability. Each loop iteration has a separate path scope, so over-unrolling a rejected tail does not shift draw numbering after the loop.

call site + scoped occurrence + expansion lane
                     ↓
                   DrawId
                     ↓
spine + role + parameters + observation mode → NodeId
                                               ↓
                         invocation seed → sampling seed

Different possible worlds of one hoisted continuation share the logical draw, but their different prompts produce different node identities and seeds. Reissuing the same node preserves its identity and seed while obtaining a fresh physical request ID.

problem_key labels logs. invocation_key participates in identity scoping; pair it consistently when a controlled comparison must reproduce one logical invocation. A stable seed alone is not a proof that every engine environment emits identical tokens.

docs.title: Tool identity excludes observations
docs.text:
A tool node is identified by its tool name, canonical JSON arguments, draw, and effect contract. Arguments containing Val objects are resolved before hashing. Invalid or non-canonical JSON is rejected; sequence handles cannot be smuggled into argument dictionaries.

Projection names and implementations identify observation views independently of the tool body. Adding a projection must not execute the same logical body again. Each named projection is cached and evaluated once, and its image is encoded lazily when a prompt actually needs it.

An after= edge changes scheduling order, not body identity. Likewise, an observation guess does not become the actual tool execution's identity.

docs.title: Four-valued guards
docs.text:
A guard is a conjunction of decision literals. While evaluating it, the runtime can observe:

Value Meaning Effect on a conjunction False A required alternative was rejected Dominates everything; the world cannot survive Pending At least one required decision is unresolved Defers failure publication because the world may still be rejected Failed A relevant decision failed Observable once no false or pending literal masks it True Every required condition is satisfied The guard permits commitment

The precedence is false, then pending, then failed, then true. For example, a failed inner judge must not fail a program whose outer decision later rejects that entire branch. When several unmasked failures exist, decision creation order provides a stable cause.

Decisions check their own entry guards before consuming rankings. This prevents a decision in an impossible world from publishing an otherwise irrelevant error.

docs.title: Why identity is shared with the compiler
docs.text:
The static compiler uses the same core chunk encoders to precompute identity prefixes. It does not maintain a parallel approximation of the hashing scheme. Dynamic holes are supplied later; runtime parity tests check that finalizing a compiled prefix agrees with live tracing.

The independent serial reference also shares identity helpers, while using different control-flow execution. That makes disagreements about which logical work survives visible instead of comparing unrelated random draws.

Source: ir.py, guards.py, values.py, and context.py.

docs.title: Prediction and optimization
docs.text: Several independent mechanisms use the word “speculation.” Establish what is being predicted, how it is verified, and whether it changes the algorithm before combining their settings or measurements.

docs.title: Four mechanisms at different levels
docs.text:
Mechanism What runs early What validates it Configuration Agent branch speculation Continuations of unresolved choices The program's original selection guards SpecConfig.enabled, window, budget Tool observation prediction A next turn built from a candidate observation The tool's declared observation policy ToolDef(obs=..., guess=...) vLLM token drafting Candidate tokens inside one generation request The engine's token-verification procedure Engine drafter configuration Score-bound truncation A candidate stops before completing A valid bound proves it cannot enter the selected top-k selection_bounds or choose(bound=...)

The first three preserve their respective output contracts through verification. Bound truncation defines an algorithm that permits early stopping under a proof obligation; it must be configured consistently in both speculation arms.

docs.title: Tool observation prediction
docs.text:
A predictor proposes a literal, asynchronous value, or symbolic sequence for the next observation. The actual tool still runs under its effect contract. Exact and projected policies compare against the real image, falling back to a real-result hole on a miss.

Sequence candidates additionally need token-segmentation agreement before their symbolic provenance can be retained. Matching visible text alone does not establish that a token-wire continuation has the same prompt.

The default draft predictor uses a small same-role model request: a 32-token budget, temperature 0.4, and top-p 0.9. Its initial candidate count is two, clipped by available capacity. Runtime-local calibration uses observed costs and outcomes; it needs at least four samples and freezes after its bounded 32-sample calibration period.

Explicit observation or guess arguments change whether this default is active; see the ToolDef defaults. Slow predictors are cut off when the real observation is ready, so prediction should not extend the critical path indefinitely.

Predictor construction runs in an advisory scope. It can use ordinary model primitives and declared-speculable tools, but cannot introduce unknown effects. Exceptions caused by invalid predictor code are distinct from ordinary misses.

docs.title: Funding hints and preemption
docs.text:
Dynamic hints influence priority and can propagate to descendants. A loser prediction may demote or cancel a speculative attempt to reclaim capacity, but the logical node remains eligible to reissue if it later becomes demanded or committed.

With ev_gate=True, funding estimates:

expected value = probability of commitment × time potentially saved
                 − estimated interference cost

Inputs come from runtime observations such as decision stalls and engine step timing. Before enough stall data exists, admission uses the probability floor, default 0.05. Demanded work is exempt to preserve liveness. These are estimates for resource allocation, not correctness evidence.

With spec_preempt=True, a better eligible speculative request may reclaim a saturated slot from a strictly worse speculative request. The policy protects committed, demanded, and nearly completed work, and bounds churn. A preempted victim returns to pending with its original identity.

Both features are off by default.

docs.title: Warm a prefix without creating a semantic result
docs.text:
judge_prefetch=True enables low-priority cache-warming requests when branch speculation is also enabled. They generate at most one token and discard the output. They have telemetry counters, but no semantic node identity or ledger result.

prefetch_on_stream(source, build, model="judge") supports a future consumer whose prompt is a transformation of partial text. build runs on the runtime event loop: keep it fast and pure. The public helper requires the text wire and is inert in serial execution.

Prefetch may reduce later prefill cost. It cannot make a consumer's missing data dependency disappear.

docs.title: Use score bounds only with a valid proof
docs.text:
Suppose a member has an upper bound on its final score. The runtime may truncate it when at least k rivals have resolved final scores strictly greater than that bound. Equality is insufficient because a tie could still affect selection.

The bound must remain valid for every allowed truncation point. A monotone-looking intermediate statistic is not automatically a valid upper bound on the score your selection actually uses.

selection_bounds(pool, bounds, k) opens a contest before scoring. Attach score values as they are created, then pass the contest to choose(..., bound=contest). A member with None as its bound is exempt from truncation but can still supply evidence against rivals.

A truncated engine node becomes done with finish_reason="bound"; it is not a preempted request waiting to resume. Keep this rule in both A/B arms and ensure no surviving computation consumes a losing candidate's truncated bytes. Differential diagnostics accommodate the permitted differences only within that algorithmic contract.

Source: predictor.py, scheduler.py, and selection-bound lowering.

docs.title: Scheduling and commitment
docs.text: The scheduler answers two different questions: can a request execute now? and can its result become part of the surviving program? Input readiness answers the first; guard resolution answers the second.

docs.title: Admission in one table
docs.text:
Data Guard Scheduler behavior Missing True or pending Wait for dependencies Ready True Enqueue as committed work, at highest request priority Ready Pending Consider speculative issue within funding and physical capacity Any False Squash; cancel an active engine attempt Any Unmasked failure Fail the dependent work

The runtime maintains a pending index rather than rescanning every historical record on every update. Decisions, data completions, hints, and capacity changes trigger reevaluation.

docs.title: Read the state correctly
docs.text:
An engine record moves through states such as pending, issued, done, squashed, and failed. Commitment is a separate property. A speculative request can be done while waiting for a guard.

There are separate completion and commitment futures. Eligible speculative descendants can use completed data before it commits, but public forcing and unknown-effect bodies wait for the appropriate commitment conditions.

This is why “the request finished” does not prove “the result was published.” The ledger records both timing and final disposition.

docs.title: Bound speculative work
docs.text:
The main controls are SpecConfig.window and max_spec_inflight:

  • The window bounds unresolved guard depth eligible for speculation. It does not count tokens or Python stack depth.
  • The budget limits concurrent funded speculative requests. It is distinct from an engine's total request capacity.

depth1_unmetered=True exempts depth-one continuations from the speculative budget, but does not create physical engine capacity. Deeper work remains metered. A static plan can replace the global depth rule for matched decisions with per-decision bounds and sibling budgets.

Among speculative candidates, the scheduler favors demanded work, shallower guards, lower rank sums, stronger dynamic hints, then registration order. Committed work takes precedence over all of them. When needed, committed requests can reclaim capacity from speculative attempts on the same engine.

docs.title: Effects have a separate execution lane
docs.text:
Python op calls use a control-plane pool. Tool bodies use a dedicated pool and tool scheduler, avoiding a single FIFO queue that could trap committed work behind speculative tool calls.

Unknown-effect operations wait for their guard and bound dependencies to commit. Unknown tools are fenced before body dispatch. Speculable tools can run early within the tool scheduler's own use of the window and budget settings.

Runtime.run drains effect obligations before returning, including on exceptional exits, subject to its configured drain timeout. Runtime.submit is a lower-level asynchronous interface; it should not be treated as an interchangeable cleanup boundary. Closing a runtime releases the scheduler, pools, and engines.

docs.title: Cancellation does not change identity
docs.text:
Cancelling an engine request aborts the physical attempt. If capacity preemption later allows it to run again, it uses the same logical node and seed with a new request ID. Old events are fenced from the new attempt.

A losing guard is different: squashed work has no surviving obligation to reissue. A running Python tool may finish after cancellation because general Python callables cannot be forcibly interrupted; its result still cannot make a rejected branch commit.

docs.title: Retry the right failures
docs.text:
Failure Current policy Committed engine request failure Up to three attempts in the request retry path Repeated speculative request failure After five failures, defer until commitment rather than fail an unresolved world immediately Deterministic projection failure Do not retry; defer publication while its guard is pending Unknown tool body failure No automatic retry Speculable tool body failure Up to three attempts per phase; commitment allows a fresh committed retry phase after speculative failures Physical engine death Fence all sibling attempts in that engine epoch, drain, and rebuild within the runtime restart limit

The default engine restart limit is one. Engine death is process-wide, so treating it as a failure of only the request that noticed it would leave sibling requests attached to a dead process.

A decision watchdog prevents a ranking or continuation condition that never resolves from leaving guards pending forever. Both decision and effect-drain timeouts are configurable.

docs.title: Keep optimization separate from semantics
docs.text:
Expected-value funding, dynamic hints, cache prefetch, and speculative slot preemption alter admission or priority. They must not remove the obligation to execute a surviving node. A score bound that permanently truncates a candidate has a different contract; see prediction and optimization.

Source: scheduler.py, tool_scheduler.py, and runtime.py.

docs.title: Streaming tool calls
docs.text:
The local adapter can dispatch a tool when its complete call becomes available, before the assistant turn finishes. It must do so without inventing partial arguments, delivering a call twice after a retry, or committing a continuation based on a call prefix that later grows.

Read tools and observations first. This page explains the machinery behind that interface.

docs.title: One assistant round
docs.text:
Render conversation with the engine's template
                  ↓
Generate tokens → native parser produces call fragments
                  ↓
Complete JSON arguments → reserve a real tool execution
                  ↓
Run the tool ──────────── predict an observation, start a guarded next turn
                  ↓                         ↓
Project the real result ────────── verify the candidate
                  ↓
Retain a matching continuation, or use the concrete observation

The arrows describe the local streamed path. The remote adapter publishes semantic calls after terminal derendering.

docs.title: Freeze the projection before generation
docs.text:
A tool-stream projection declares the model family, parser, rendering contract, and structural constraints before an engine node is registered. Capability identity is checked throughout execution. Changing a parser after a request's identity is established would change what that request means.

The adapter uses vLLM's tool-parser implementations and family-specific profiles. It does not replace model grammars with one generic handwritten parser. Unsupported model, parser, or reasoning combinations are rejected by the profile resolver.

Each attempt gets a fresh parser state. Immutable vocabulary information can be memoized, but incremental parse state cannot be shared across requests or retries.

docs.title: Close arguments before constructing the tool
docs.text:
A lexical JSON closure scanner tracks nesting, strings, and escapes incrementally. It identifies when a candidate argument object might be complete; strict JSON decoding remains authoritative. Duplicate keys, invalid values, and malformed argument objects are rejected.

The tracer reserves structural slots and future draw positions before all call bytes exist. A real tool node is created only after its tool name and canonical arguments are known. This avoids provisional tool identities that would later mutate as more bytes arrive.

The distinction also applies to the next assistant turn: reserving its draw position does not mean its engine node has already been registered. Early registration needs a closed call and a valid candidate observation.

docs.title: Make delivery stable across retries
docs.text:
A per-request journal records emitted calls in prefix order. A retried generation must replay the same already-published prefix. Matching replay does not dispatch the same call again; divergence raises a projection error.

At the end of the turn, full parsing is cross-checked against the streamed interpretation. This can discover a late failure, but it cannot undo external effects from calls already delivered. The effect fence and journal are therefore part of the correctness boundary, not optional parser conveniences.

docs.title: Verify that the call prefix is final
docs.text:
A continuation predicted after one call assumes that no additional calls belong to that round. If another call appears, the shorter-prefix continuation is squashed. It cannot commit merely because its first observation prediction was correct.

For bounded multi-call rounds, the implementation builds one representative vector across call slots, with work proportional to the slot count. It does not construct the Cartesian product of every call's observation candidates. A miss or unsupported shape falls back to concrete observations.

The max_calls template includes overflow handling. Exceeding the speculative shape bound introduces a barrier; it does not silently discard the remaining actual calls.

docs.title: Keep policies local and selectors constrained
docs.text:
A ToolDef is a reusable prototype. Each call obtains a new policy session before registering its projection. The default Policy.new_session makes a shallow copy. A policy with nested mutable per-call state must override it and allocate that state explicitly.

The policy protocol has four stages:

Method Responsibility new_session() Create call-local policy state project(raw) Purely reduce the real result to its observation image slots(state, call) Declare candidate observations before selecting on the real image select(image, slots) Return a declared slot index, or no selection, exactly once

image is lazy. Constant policies and hole-only policies need not read or encode it. This matters in remote mode, where unnecessary token conversion can cost an extra network request.

Selectors cannot inject an undeclared result through the selection channel. Custom policy errors are errors, not prediction misses. hole()—also spelled open()—declares a slot filled by the real observation; JSON None is a literal null representative, not a hole.

Source: tool_stream.py, tool_slots.py, tools.py, and policy.py.

docs.title: Core concepts
docs.text: The essential distinction is between a symbolic handle, which describes work, and a concrete value, which lets Python inspect its result. Keeping data symbolic gives the tracer room to construct future work.

docs.title: Three handles
docs.text:
Handle What it represents Typical producer Seq A prompt state: literals, generated output, and possibly tool observations lit, cat, infer Val A future Python value, with its dependency and guard information op, out_text, collect Choice One rank of a selection whose member may not yet be known choose(...)[rank], gate

You normally import the DSL functions from agentir; the handle implementations live in agentir.core.values. Handles belong to their tracing context. Do not carry them from one runtime.run invocation into another.

docs.title: A sequence includes its prompt
docs.text:
After answer = infer(prompt), the sequence contains prompt plus the new output. Consequently:

full_state = text(answer)       # Val[str]: prompt and output
generated = out_text(answer)    # Val[str]: the generated tail

Use out_text for answer extraction. Use the sequence itself for a continuation:

followup = infer(cat(answer, lit("\nExplain the last step.")))

This preserves the producer as a symbolic dependency. Converting to a string and rebuilding a literal waits for data and removes that structural connection.

fmt(template, **parts) is a convenience for named composition. It can preserve sequence provenance where the corresponding string formatting would materialize values. Keep templates simple; it is not a replacement for the full Python formatting language.

docs.title: Decisions select indices
docs.text:
choose(pool, by=ranking, k=1) expects a ranked list of distinct integer positions into the pool. Rank zero is the first position in that ranking, not necessarily pool position zero.

selected = choose(candidates, by=ranking, k=1)[0]

Selection does not splice arbitrary returned text into the graph. It routes to handles that already exist. This is what makes their possible continuations available before selection finishes.

Rankings must be long enough for k, contain no duplicate or out-of-range indices, and use integers rather than booleans. Duplicate members in the selection pool are rejected.

docs.title: Guards determine whether work survives
docs.text:
A guard is a conjunction of selection conditions, such as “the outer judge chooses branch 1, and the next loop round is entered.” A node can have all its data and still have an unresolved guard.

The scheduler may execute that node speculatively. It commits only when the guard is true. False guards squash their work. Errors from a branch that is eventually rejected are not automatically errors of the surviving program; guard evaluation defines the precise behavior.

docs.title: Readiness and publication are separate
docs.text:
op(fn, ..., pure=True) can compute on available speculative inputs. The default, pure=False, waits for its entry guard and bound dependencies to commit before running an effectful function.

force(value) is the public publication boundary. It waits for the value and the conditions under which it may be observed. Calling a low-level future's .result() merely to obtain ready data is not a substitute for that boundary.

Python if, bool, and iteration cannot decide based on an unresolved symbolic value. Use guarded control flow, or intentionally force a value when the program really must branch in Python.

docs.title: Text and token wires
docs.text:
The wire is the representation used for prompt atoms. The text wire carries strings. The token wire carries exact token-ID tuples and preserves model-specific chat boundaries. Autonomous tool loops require the token wire.

Both wires use the same conceptual IR. Their representations are not interchangeable inside a runtime. See wire and model compatibility.

docs.title: A small vocabulary, several algorithms
docs.text: expand → evaluate → choose → infer describes candidate selection and refinement. loop adds bounded, data-dependent repetition. Tools add effect contracts and observation policies. The algorithm guide shows how these mechanisms compose without introducing a different scheduler for each algorithm.

docs.title: Your first program
docs.text:
This program samples four short answers, selects the most common numeric answer, and asks for a one-sentence conclusion. The last request can begin while the vote is unresolved.

You need the local installation and a working GPU engine to run it. The complete version lives in examples/quickstart.py.

docs.title: The complete program
docs.text:
Save the following as first_program.py in your checkout:

import re
from collections import Counter

from agentir import (
    SpecConfig, cat, choose, collect, expand, force,
    infer, lit, make_runtime, op, out_text,
)


def extract_number(answer):
    numbers = re.findall(r"-?\d+", answer or "")
    return numbers[-1] if numbers else ""


def rank_by_vote(answers):
    counts = Counter(answer for answer in answers if answer)
    return sorted(
        range(len(answers)),
        key=lambda i: -counts.get(answers[i], 0),
    )


def program():
    prompt = lit(
        "Q: A pen costs 3 dollars. How much do 5 pens cost? "
        "Reason briefly, then give the number.\nA:"
    )
    candidates = expand(prompt, 4, max_tokens=96)
    answers = collect([
        op(extract_number, out_text(candidate), pure=True)
        for candidate in candidates
    ])
    ranking = op(rank_by_vote, answers, pure=True)
    selected = choose(candidates, by=ranking, k=1)[0]
    conclusion = infer(
        cat(selected, lit("\nSo, in one sentence:")),
        max_tokens=32,
    )
    return force(out_text(conclusion))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with make_runtime(
        model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct",
        spec=SpecConfig(window=2),
        engine_args={"max_model_len": 2048, "gpu_memory_utilization": 0.5},
    ) as runtime:
        print(runtime.run(program, problem_key="first-program"))

Run it from the activated environment:

python first_program.py

It prints the final generated conclusion. The exact wording depends on the model and execution environment; the intended arithmetic answer is 15 dollars.

docs.title: 1. Generate candidates without reading them
docs.text:
lit creates a literal prompt handle. expand(prompt, 4) creates four separate sampling draws that share a prompt prefix. Each result is a Seq: the original prompt followed by that draw's generated output.

Creating these handles does not require the tracer to wait for their strings. The engine can execute ready requests while Python continues building the program.

docs.title: 2. Evaluate through asynchronous values
docs.text:
out_text(candidate) describes the generated tail of a candidate. Each op waits for its input, extracts a number, and produces a Val. collect gathers those values in candidate order, and another op produces a ranking of indices.

Both functions are marked pure=True because they are deterministic computations with no external effects. That declaration lets eligible speculative work use their results before commitment. It is a contract you provide, not a purity check performed by Python.

docs.title: 3. Preserve the choice
docs.text:
choose(..., k=1)[0] represents rank zero of an unresolved selection. It preserves all possible candidate identities until the ranking resolves.

Passing this handle to cat and infer lets the tracer construct one continuation per possible selected candidate. Each continuation needs its candidate's output, but its prompt does not depend on the vote result. The scheduler can therefore run it early if capacity and speculation budgets allow.

If you instead force the ranking and use ordinary Python indexing, you make selection a tracing barrier and lose this overlap opportunity.

docs.title: 4. Publish one answer
docs.text:
force(out_text(conclusion)) waits for the selected continuation and the decisions that allow it to be observed. Losing continuations do not become return values.

This small vote is deliberately cheap, so it may leave little useful overlap. The example teaches the programming model; it is not a performance benchmark. A model-based judge or a slower decision may create a larger opportunity.

docs.title: Inspect what happened
docs.text:
Before leaving the runtime's with block, you can inspect the invocation's ledger:

rows = runtime.ledger_for("first-program")
print("issued speculatively:", sum(row.speculative for row in rows))
print("committed:", sum(row.disposition == "committed" for row in rows))

A zero speculative count can be legitimate: the vote may resolve before a continuation is ready. Learn to distinguish this from a scheduling problem in timelines and diagnostics.

Next, read core concepts for the handles and boundaries used throughout the API.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: The AgentIR package requires Python 3.11 or newer. Model execution uses the pinned vLLM 0.24.0 adapter. You can explore the API and compile program shapes without installing vLLM or loading model weights.

docs.title: Get the source
docs.text:
Run these commands from a shell with Python available:

git clone https://github.com/sunyxedu/AgentIR.git
cd AgentIR
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
agentir list

agentir list prints the built-in algorithms and datasets. It does not load a model. An editable installation lets the examples and CLI use the code in your checkout.

docs.title: Choose how to execute models
docs.text:
Local vLLMRemote vLLMExplore without a GPU

On a supported Linux GPU host, install the engine extra into an environment compatible with vLLM:

python -m pip install -e '.[vllm]'
python examples/quickstart.py Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct

The first model use downloads weights if needed and starts the engine. The example's small context and memory settings are a starting point, not a promise that every GPU can run it. Engine installation, drivers, available memory, and access to the requested model must all be in place.

See models and vLLM for device placement, chat rendering, and token-wire compatibility.

Keep the base installation on the client. The remote adapter uses the standard library and delegates tokenization, rendering, and parsing to the server:

from agentir import make_remote_runtime

runtime = make_remote_runtime(
    model="Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct",
    base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
)

Constructing the runtime does not establish that the server is usable. First use performs a handshake. The endpoint must provide the AgentIR certificate middleware and Tier-1 routes described in remote execution; a generic chat-completions endpoint is insufficient.

Install development dependencies to run the engine-independent tests:

python -m pip install -e '.[dev]'
python -m pytest tests/test_ir.py tests/test_compile_shape.py

See static shape compilation for a complete program you can inspect without a model. This validates graph construction; it does not execute model inference.

docs.title: Keep the engine entry point guarded
docs.text:
vLLM starts subprocesses. Put runtime creation and execution behind the normal Python main guard:

def main():
    # Create and use the runtime here.
    pass

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Always close a runtime, preferably with a with statement. A runtime owns event-loop and worker threads as well as engine resources.

docs.title: Other environments
docs.text:
The Harbor integration requires Python 3.12+ and the separate harbor extra, pinned to Harbor 0.16.1. Install the adapter in the same environment as the harbor command.

To build this documentation, use the isolated documentation setup. It has no GPU dependency.

Continue with your first program.

docs.title: Algorithms
docs.text:
The built-in algorithms are ordinary AgentIR programs. They are useful both as runnable baselines and as examples of where weak control dependencies appear in an agent workflow.

Run agentir list for the available names. Import implementations from agentir.algos, or select one with agentir bench --algo NAME.

docs.title: Choose a program structure
docs.text:
Algorithm What it does Where overlap can appear self_consistency Sample answers, vote on extracted answers, optionally explain the winner The explanation can continue from candidates before the vote resolves best_of_n Sample candidates, score each with a judge, return the selected original answer Candidate generation and scoring overlap; this implementation has no final polish request heavy Generate several answers, use a comparative judge, continue from the selected answer The final continuation can overlap the comparative decision cascade Produce and review a draft, then select escalation or polishing behavior Alternative continuations can be constructed before the review selects one beam_search Repeatedly expand a bounded beam and select the next beam Next-round continuations can run under unresolved beam selections sal_beam Search by scored reasoning steps and aggregate completed answers Available overlap depends on step boundaries and materialization needed for scoring reflexion Review and revise until accepted or the iteration bound is reached Future iterations are traced under continue guards mcts Maintain search statistics, select a frontier, roll out, and backpropagate Finite frontier choices expose local speculation; iterations settle their state updates

The table describes the checked-in implementations. Sharing an algorithm name with a paper does not establish identical prompts, scoring, or stopping rules.

docs.title: Read a representative algorithm
docs.text:
Start with heavy.py if you want to see the complete generate–judge–continue pattern. Read self_consistency.py for Python value operations, and reflexion.py for loop.

common.py supplies prompt construction, answer normalization, score parsing, and ranking helpers. These functions affect measured task accuracy: a successful model request can still yield an unparseable or incorrectly normalized answer.

docs.title: Scoring changes the dependency graph
docs.text:
Beam search can score using log probabilities, judge generations, or a process reward model (PRM). These choices need different data:

  • Log probabilities come from the generation's observation mode. They must be requested as part of that node.
  • A judge continuation can often consume the candidate's symbolic spine directly.
  • A transformed PRM prompt may need concrete candidate text before it can be constructed. That creates a data barrier; cache prefetch can help prefill, but cannot erase the dependency.

The SAL implementation also materializes step text for parts of its control flow. Do not assume every algorithm is entirely trace-ahead or accepted by the static compiler.

docs.title: Keep algorithm changes separate from scheduler changes
docs.text:
Candidate count, beam width, stopping rules, scoring aggregation, token budgets, and bound_commit change the algorithm or its output contract. The speculation window, funding budget, and priority policies control how its graph is scheduled.

For an A/B comparison of branch speculation, hold the algorithm fixed. In particular, if a valid bound allows early truncation, enable that same algorithmic rule in both arms. See benchmarking.

Function defaults and CLI defaults can differ: for example, the shared CLI --k default is 6. Use the CLI reference and the function signature for the entry point you actually run.

docs.title: Branching and loops
docs.text: Use choose, gate, and loop when a decision determines which already-describable work survives. Use ordinary Python control flow when the next request genuinely cannot be constructed without inspecting a concrete result.

docs.title: Continue through a selection
docs.text:
The common pattern keeps the ranking asynchronous:

candidates = expand(prompt, 3, max_tokens=128)
scores = collect([
    op(score_answer, out_text(candidate), pure=True)
    for candidate in candidates
])
ranking = op(rank_scores, scores, pure=True)
best = choose(candidates, by=ranking, k=1)[0]
answer = infer(cat(best, lit("\nGive a concise conclusion.")), max_tokens=64)

Here score_answer and rank_scores are application functions; the latter returns candidate indices in preferred order. The continuation of each candidate waits for that candidate's data, while its selection guard may remain pending.

Request k > 1 to retain several ranks. Each choose result is a rank-specific Choice, so downstream requests preserve which rank and member they depend on.

docs.title: Gate optional work
docs.text:
gate(value, condition) keeps the value when the condition is true. It returns a choice with a single surviving alternative; a false condition has no fallback result.

keep = op(needs_more_detail, out_text(draft), pure=True)
optional = infer(
    cat(gate(draft, keep), lit("\nAdd the missing detail.")),
    max_tokens=128,
)

If keep is false, forcing optional raises Squashed. Use a selection with explicit alternatives when you need a result on both outcomes. A gate is particularly useful inside a larger guarded computation whose rejected result is never published.

docs.title: Iterate while preserving the stop decision
docs.text:
loop(init, body, max_iters, lookahead=None) expects body(state) to return (next_state, continue_condition). The condition can be a Val; do not force it inside the body just to decide whether to continue.

def revise(state):
    review = infer(cat(state, lit("\nReview this answer.")), max_tokens=96)
    keep_going = op(needs_revision, out_text(review), pure=True)
    revised = infer(cat(review, lit("\nWrite a revised answer.")), max_tokens=192)
    return revised, keep_going

result = loop(draft, revise, max_iters=3)

needs_revision is your pure parser of the review. The runtime can construct later rounds under the assumption that the loop continues, bounded by the lookahead.

The returned state is the entering state

When a round's condition says stop, loop returns the state that entered that round, not the next_state it proposed. If every condition is true through max_iters, it returns the last next state. In the example, a review that accepts the current answer returns that answer.

Round zero uses the loop's entry guard. Round one additionally requires round zero's condition to be true, and so on. A round's condition producer therefore never waits on its own decision. Each iteration also has a separate draw scope, so speculative extra rounds do not renumber later work.

The default lookahead is the speculation window when enabled and zero when disabled. The tracer eventually waits to determine the loop's return value; loop does not make arbitrary Python execution asynchronous.

docs.title: Understand the boundaries
docs.text:
Situation Consequence Appropriate response force a ranking before choose Selection becomes a tracing barrier Pass the ranking Val directly when possible Convert a generated answer to a new literal The tracer waits for text and loses spine provenance Continue from its Seq, or use fmt for supported composition Concatenate two independent unresolved choices Current lowering does not form their Cartesian product Restructure around one decision or introduce an explicit barrier Branch in Python on a handle Symbolic truth conversion fails Use guarded control flow, or deliberately materialize data Put external effects inside op(..., pure=True) The purity contract is violated Use the default effectful op, or an appropriately declared tool

The tracer also limits hoisting fan-out to prevent accidental graph explosion. If a program exceeds that limit, reduce speculative breadth or introduce a deliberate phase boundary.

For an implementation of iterative refinement, read reflexion.py. For how the window is funded, continue with scheduling.

docs.title: Remote execution
docs.text:
make_remote_runtime runs the AgentIR tracer and scheduler on the client while a certified vLLM Tier-1 server owns tokenization, chat rendering, model execution, and tool parsing. The client needs neither local vLLM nor a local tokenizer.

This is a specific token-in/token-out protocol. A server exposing only an OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint does not satisfy it.

docs.title: Prepare the server
docs.text:
Install the same AgentIR checkout into the server's vLLM 0.24.0 environment, so its middleware is importable. The following is a server launch template for the Qwen3-Coder tool family; choose context, memory, and model revision settings appropriate to your hardware:

python -m vllm.entrypoints.openai.api_server \
  --model Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8000 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml \
  --middleware agentir.execution.vllm_certificate.middleware \
  --scheduling-policy priority \
  --enable-prefix-caching \
  --generation-config vllm

The parser must match the selected model family. The checked-in experiment launcher is hephaestus_terminal_bench_paired.sbatch; its cluster paths, resource allocations, and experimental locks are specific to that environment.

Probe the certificate route after startup:

curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/agentir/tier1/certificate

An unavailable certificate or incompatible server is a setup failure. Do not substitute stock render routes to bypass the handshake.

docs.title: Connect the client
docs.text:
from agentir import force, infer, lit, make_remote_runtime, out_text


def program():
    return force(out_text(infer(lit("The capital of France is"), max_tokens=32)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with make_remote_runtime(
        model="Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct",
        base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000",
    ) as runtime:
        print(runtime.run(program))

The remote runtime always uses the token wire and exposes main with a judge alias. A trailing /v1 on the endpoint is normalized to the server base. Pass an API key or headers through the constructor when the server requires them.

docs.title: Follow one request
docs.text:
Stage Route Purpose Handshake /version and /v1/agentir/tier1/certificate Check the pinned version and bind the server contract Render /v1/agentir/tier1/render Convert the conversation into exact prompt tokens and request settings Generate /inference/v1/generate Execute token-in/token-out inference Derender /v1/agentir/tier1/derender Interpret the final tokens using the certified parser and template Token conversion /tokenize, /detokenize Provide the remote token-wire operations

The certificate binds the model and tokenizer revisions, template and parser implementation, and required features. Requests and responses carry certificate-digest and instance-ID headers. An instance change invalidates cached assumptions even if the visible model name stays the same.

certificate_mode="required" is the supported default. expected_certificate_sha256 can pin an exact deployment contract for a controlled experiment. Version checks alone cannot establish parser or rendering equivalence.

docs.title: Know the streaming boundary
docs.text:
The client reads generation SSE incrementally, but buffers the semantic tool projection until generation and derendering finish. Remote tool calls are published at the terminal boundary. It does not provide the local adapter's early per-call dispatch during model decoding.

After a call is available, a predicted next turn can still overlap the real tool execution. Keep these two overlap opportunities separate when comparing local and remote runs.

docs.title: Cancellation and caching
docs.text:
Cancellation closes the exact active HTTP connection. Successful ordinary JSON requests can reuse pooled HTTP/1.1 connections; generation SSE connections are not reused. A bounded render cache stores successful results for exact canonical requests within the certified instance, with singleflight coordination for concurrent identical renders.

The default render cache holds 128 entries. Restart or handshake changes fence old cache entries and attempts. The client's restart path can re-handshake; it does not launch or repair the external service.

Capabilities that cannot be safely checked remotely are rejected. For example, the current adapter cannot perform the required structural_tag preflight and fails closed for that feature. Higher provider protocol tiers discussed in research material are not additional implemented backends.

Source: remote.py, vllm_certificate.py, and remote protocol tests.

docs.title: Tools and observations
docs.text: A tool adds two separate contracts to an agent program: when its body may execute, and what information its result contributes to the conversation. Define them separately. A predictable result does not make a side effect safe to repeat.

docs.title: Define a tool
docs.text:
The public autonomous loop is infer(task, tools=..., max_turns=...). It uses the token wire and the engine's own chat template and tool parser.

This complete example exposes an in-memory lookup. Replace the model with a supported tool-capable model that fits your environment:

from agentir import Exact, ToolDef, force, infer, make_runtime, out_text

CAPITALS = {"France": "Paris", "Japan": "Tokyo"}


def lookup_capital(args):
    return CAPITALS.get(args["country"], "Unknown")


def program():
    response = infer(
        "Use the lookup tool to find the capital of France.",
        tools={
            "lookup_capital": ToolDef(
                lookup_capital,
                effect="speculable",
                obs=Exact(),
                description="Look up a country's capital in a small local table.",
                input_schema={
                    "type": "object",
                    "properties": {"country": {"type": "string"}},
                    "required": ["country"],
                    "additionalProperties": False,
                },
            ),
        },
        max_turns=4,
        max_tokens=128,
    )
    return force(out_text(response))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with make_runtime(
        model="Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct",
        wire="tokens",
    ) as runtime:
        print(runtime.run(program))

The callable receives one argument dictionary, not keyword arguments. input_schema is the JSON Schema for that dictionary; AgentIR adds the provider's function wrapper. The returned Seq is the final assistant turn of the tool loop.

docs.title: Decide whether execution can be speculative
docs.text:
effect When the body can run Your contract "unknown" (default) After its guard is true and required ordering has settled The runtime must fence external effects and avoid speculative execution "speculable" Under a pending guard, within the tool budget Extra executions and retries are safe; observations remain suitable for replay

Reading a fixed in-memory table is a straightforward speculable tool. A shell command, payment, file write, or changing database query needs a deliberate effect decision. The Harbor shell tool uses "unknown".

A running Python callable cannot be forcibly stopped in the general case. Cancellation can prevent a queued tool from starting, but it cannot undo a body that has already run. Unknown tools are not automatically retried. Speculable tools can be retried, so “read-only” alone may be too weak a contract if results depend on changing external state.

docs.title: Choose what the model observes
docs.text:
The policy turns the raw tool result into an observation image and selects a declared candidate observation. Images are strings or canonically rendered JSON values.

Policy Observation contract Useful when Exact() Preserve the actual image; guesses must match exactly The full result matters Ignore(text="done") Use a constant image without reading the raw result Completion matters, but result contents do not Project(alpha) Expose a pure projection of the result The model needs a stable subset or normalized form Enum(cases, by=...) Select among declared representatives or a real-result hole A finite set of outcomes is part of the tool's interface

Ignore and Project deliberately define what information the agent receives. They are semantic choices, not approximate substitutes for an exact observation.

docs.title: Add a prediction
docs.text:
A guess funds work against a possible observation while the real tool runs:

tool_definition = ToolDef(
    lookup_capital,
    effect="speculable",
    obs=Exact(),
    guess="Paris",
)

The loop verifies the projected real observation against the guess. A hit retains the candidate continuation; a miss uses the real observation. With an unknown-effect tool, the body still waits for commitment, but its predicted next model turn can overlap that body once the relevant conversation is eligible.

Defaults depend on what you specify

ToolDef(fn) supplies Exact() and a default model-based draft predictor. Supplying obs=Exact() explicitly disables that implicit predictor unless you also pass guess. Passing guess=None explicitly also disables it. This distinction matters for request budgets and baseline experiments.

Advanced guesses can be callables that construct Val or Seq candidates, including ordinary DSL model calls. These are advisory computations: unknown effects are forbidden inside predictor construction. See prediction and optimization.

docs.title: Use tools directly in the graph
docs.text:
When your program already knows the operation and its arguments, it can register a tool without asking the model to call it:

from agentir import cat, expect, force, infer, lit, tool, out_text

def program():
    result = tool(
        lookup_capital,
        {"country": "France"},
        name="lookup_capital",
        effect="speculable",
    )
    observation = expect(result, "Paris")
    answer = infer(cat(lit("The lookup returned: "), observation), max_tokens=48)
    return force(out_text(answer))

obs(handle) inserts a late-bound observation into a prompt spine. observe(handle) returns its structured projected value. ack(handle) waits for completion without reading content. classify routes exact projected images through a closed mapping; an unlisted result is an error, so use expect when misses need a fallback.

Pass after= to impose execution ordering on a direct tool. Its predecessors must settle, but their values and failures are not injected into the new tool. If failure propagation is required, express that dependency explicitly.

docs.title: Bound the conversation
docs.text:
max_turns bounds assistant rounds. max_calls bounds the speculative call-slot template for a round; the autonomous loop has an overflow barrier that handles the concrete calls at termination instead of silently dropping them. It is not a universal authorization limit on external actions. Use tool-side policy if your application requires such a limit.

For custom observation policies and early dispatch mechanics, continue with streaming tool calls. For a real terminal integration, read Harbor.

docs.title: Harbor and Terminal-Bench
docs.text:
AgentIR supplies a custom agent for Harbor 0.16.1 at agentir.integrations.harbor.agent:AgentIRHarborAgent. Harbor owns the task environment and trial lifecycle; AgentIR owns the model program and tool loop.

The default runner uses certified remote vLLM. Backend selection is explicit: a failed remote connection does not trigger local model loading.

docs.title: Install into Harbor's environment
docs.text:
Harbor requires Python 3.12 or newer. From the AgentIR checkout:

uv venv --python 3.12 .venv-harbor
source .venv-harbor/bin/activate
uv pip install -e '.[harbor]'
python -c 'import harbor; print(harbor.__version__)'

Use the same environment for the harbor executable and AgentIR's import path. Start a vLLM 0.24.0 server with the AgentIR certificate middleware, following the server setup.

docs.title: Run a trial
docs.text:
This command runs Terminal-Bench 2.0 with branch speculation disabled:

harbor run \
  --dataset terminal-bench@2.0 \
  --agent agentir.integrations.harbor.agent:AgentIRHarborAgent \
  --model openai/Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct \
  --agent-kwarg model_endpoint=http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 \
  --agent-kwarg runner_backend=remote_vllm_tier1 \
  --agent-kwarg spec_enabled=false \
  --agent-kwarg max_turns=32 \
  --agent-kwarg shell_timeout_sec=120 \
  --n-concurrent 1

Set spec_enabled=true for the speculation-on arm. This controls SpecConfig.enabled, not just the result label. Model access, Harbor's task runtime, and the dataset's environment requirements must be available before the trial can run.

For explicit local execution, pass runner_backend=in_process_vllm and install the engine into that environment. That mode ignores the remote endpoint for inference and records the selected backend in metadata.

docs.title: How shell execution crosses the boundary
docs.text:
Harbor's environment is asynchronous. The synchronous AgentIR invocation runs in a worker thread; its shell tool submits requests back to Harbor's owning event loop with asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe. Trial cancellation propagates to active environment calls.

The shell tool has effect="unknown": speculative branches cannot run shell commands. Its observation predictor proposes the common empty-success image, allowing a next model turn to overlap a real committed command. Exact image comparison decides whether that continuation survives.

The shell schema requires a non-empty command, allows cwd and timeout_sec, and rejects extra fields. The adapter caps requested timeouts at shell_timeout_sec and preserves the environment's configured default user.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
Prompt observations contain canonical JSON for stdout, stderr, return code, timeout/error state, and truncation metadata. Each output stream is bounded to 65,536 characters by default, preserving its head and tail. Full raw provider observations remain in the trial's ATIF record.

The adapter persists ATIF v1.7 trajectories, timing, command outcomes, and runner metadata. Remote records identify the normalized effective endpoint and certificate contract; API keys are represented only by whether they were configured.

Warmed runtimes are cached per exact backend and runner configuration, including the speculation arm and endpoint. The cache is reference-counted and fork-aware. Applications can call agentir.integrations.harbor.close_cached_runtimes() to close cached runtimes explicitly.
